messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Animator
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 39

# The Weight of What She Saw

Maya is twenty-one years old, a second-year animation student at a small arts college in the Pacific Northwest, far from the apartment in Houston where she grew up. She chose the distance deliberately, though she wouldn't have been able to articulate why until recently. She tells her therapist that she has always been good at drawing things that aren't quite real — creatures, fantastical worlds, characters with exaggerated expressions — and that she suspects this is not a coincidence.

She was seven the first time she remembers her father hitting her mother. She remembers the sound more than the image: the flat, terrible crack of it, and then her mother's silence, which somehow felt louder. Maya was behind the couch, having slid there during the argument, the way she had learned to do. She stayed very still. She tells her therapist she became an expert at stillness during those years — at making herself small and breathless, convinced on some level that if she didn't move, time might stop too. The violence in her home was not constant, but it was unpredictable, and unpredictability, she has come to understand, is its own kind of cruelty. It continued until she was thirteen, when her mother finally left and moved them both to her aunt's house in a different part of the city.

By the time Maya arrived at college, she believed she had left all of it behind. She was talented, driven, and genuinely excited about her work. But in her second semester, a professor played a film clip in class — a domestic drama, a scene in which a man slammed his hand against a wall near a woman's face — and something in Maya's body responded before her mind could catch up. Her heart hammered. The room felt like it was tilting. She got up and left without explanation and sat in a bathroom stall for twenty minutes, shaking, unsure what had just happened to her.

Since then, she has noticed the pattern. Raised voices in the hallway of her apartment building. The sound of something dropped or broken. A certain quality of tension in a room — something she reads in posture, in silence, in the way people hold their faces — these things send her nervous system into a state of high alert that can last for hours. She has trouble sleeping, often lying awake running through scenarios she cannot name, her body convinced there is something she needs to prepare for. She is frequently exhausted.

Her animation work has become both refuge and complication. She loses herself in it for hours, sometimes preferring the controlled world of her drawing tablet to the unpredictability of other people. Her characters tend to be solitary figures in wide, quiet landscapes. Her advisor has praised the emotional depth of her work without knowing what feeds it. But lately she has been avoiding a group project, finding reasons not to attend collaborative sessions, and her relationships with her classmates have grown thin. She wants connection but finds herself scanning interactions for signs of danger, bracing for shifts in tone, withdrawing when things feel uncertain.

She describes her childhood self with a tenderness that is also grief — the little girl behind the couch, the one who learned to read danger before she learned to read chapter books. She says she doesn't blame her mother. She says she has complicated feelings about her father that she is not ready to examine closely yet. She says she thought growing up would mean growing out of this, and she is quietly devastated to discover it doesn't work that way.

She is sitting in a therapist's office now, in a rainy city a thousand miles from Houston, trying to learn — for the first time — what it feels like to stay in the room.
